# 1 | Background

This project aims to resolve the issues within rostering for ad-hoc jobs. Currently, traditional gig-work and temporary staffing platforms often rely on a "first-come, first-served" job allocation model. 

For employers, the current system requires creating and managing multiple job listings across different sites. Additional manpower is needed to vet through applicants, and they face the issue of frequent no-shows from staff on the day of the event, leading to operational disruptions.

For employees, this model forces results in a reactive cycle of constantly monitoring for openings and potentially missed opportunities that better fit their skills, preferences, and availability. 

This fragmented, inefficient approach leads to employee frustration over inconsistent access to work and a lack of reliable fulfilment for employers.

# 2 | Problem Statement

How can we make the process of roster allocation more seamless for both employees and job seekers?

# 3 | Use Case Diagrams

There are two main actors within the system, employers and job seekers.  

Job seekers interact with the system primarily to discover and manage suitable ad-hoc job opportunities. Their three base use cases include setting preferences, indicating availability and cancelling their shift. 

For the Employer, there are three base use cases of listing jobs, rating employees and cancelling their shifts. For all of these use cases, they share the sub-use cases of signing up and creating an account, which differentiates their role in the system from the start.

## 3\. 2 | Employer User Tables

An employer can list jobs (Figure 8), either by creating individual listings or in bulk through a CSV upload. Our system also handles critical edge cases, such as a jobseeker needing to cancel a shift, an employer cancelling a job listing (Figure 9), or exporting schedules as a separate file (Figure 10). Finally, the employer may also choose to rate an employee's performance (Figure 11). 

| ID | UC7 |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Name** | Employer Posts Job Request  |
| **Description** | An employer defines the requirements for one or more shifts they need to fill for an upcoming scheduling cycle. |
| **Actors** | Employer (Primary) |
| **Triggers** | Client navigates to the "Post a Job" or "Upload Shifts" page. |
| **Preconditions** | Client is logged in and authenticated. |
| **Postconditions** | New shift records are created in the database with a status of 'OPEN'.  The shifts are now included in the next automated scheduling cycle. |
| **Error States** | Job posting fails due to invalid data (e.g., end time before start time).  For CSV uploads, data errors are flagged and  CSV will not be imported.  |
| **Flow** | Client selects "Post a New Job".  System displays the job creation form.  Client enters the job title, required dates and times, pay rate, location, and number of staff needed. Client clicks "Submit Job".  System validates the data and creates new records in the Shifts table.  System displays a "Shifts successfully posted" confirmation message. |
| **Alternative Flow** | Upload via CSV:  1a. Client selects "Upload from CSV".  2a. Client uploads a CSV file with the required shift details. 3\.  3a. System parses the file and validates the data for each row. 4a. System creates new records in the Shifts table for each valid row.  5a. System displays a confirmation message, noting any rows that failed to import. |

# 4 | Risks and Mitigations

There are three main risks identified within the project. Firstly, the ambitious number of features needed to be implemented. To mitigate this, we are prioritising the  core functionalities of roster allocation, which includes features such as indication of preferences and availability, and the creation of new job listings. Other optional features, such as a two-way rating system will be implemented only after the MVP is complete. 

Second, there is a higher workload from creating two distinct user interfaces. We are mitigating this by reusing design components between user interfaces where possible and finalizing our designs in Figma first to streamline front-end development. For example, features like the navigation bar can be reused across both user interfaces and adjusted slightly to suit the specific needs of each user.

Finally, to address any unfamiliarity with new programming frameworks such as react, our strategy is to substitute complex solutions with simpler, effective ones if we face time constraints, ensuring we always have a working product. For example, instead of creating a new allocation algorithm model using machine learning, we attempt to implement existing algorithms for roster allocations instead.

# 6 | Development Model

The chosen development model is incremental. This allows us to break down the project into smaller, manageable components, like the dashboard, login, and analytics, and progressively improve upon them with each iteration. Moreover, this will allow for testing of individual components before integration, which is crucial for managing the complexity of the project.

# 7 | Discussion With Instructors

Discussions with the instructors allowed for further refinement of ideas. Firstly, the roster allocation process was streamlined into a simplified 3-step operational flow: Availability, Allocation, and Notification. An extra confirmation step was removed to make the process seamless. For notifications, email was chosen as the main mode of communication between stakeholders.

To address the issue of slow allocation with a single weekly cycle, we've introduced a mid-week cycle, which increases the platform's responsiveness and provides more opportunities for job seekers.

Finally, to improve the quality and reliability of the workforce, employers have the option to rate job seekers post-shift to maintain quality on the platform. Job seekers can also view their ratings, which directly affect their job eligibility.

# 8 | Timeline

The project timeline was structured to ensure steady progress over the following weeks. Currently, in Weeks 5 and 6, the main focus will be finalizing Figma wireframes and the backend schema. We will also begin the initial build of both the front-end and the database. 

Weeks 7 and 8 will be dedicated to connecting the front-end to the back-end, setting up user authentication, and preparing for the second checkoff. 

The later weeks, from 9 to 12, will be focused on iterative development, comprehensive testing, and preparing our final report and documentation, culminating in our final presentation in Week 13\.
